questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x+y)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(1,-1)$ to the point $B(-3,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i-j$ and $b=-3\,i+j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(i-j)+t[-3\,i+j-(i-j)] \\  & =(i-j)+t(-4\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(1-4t)\,i+(2t-1)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=1-4t,\,y=2t-1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(x+y)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y\,j \\  & =(1-4t+(2t-1))\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡((2t-1)\pi )\,j \\  & =-2t\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡((2t-1)\pi )\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-4t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)j \\  & =-4\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-2t\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡((2t-1)\pi )\,j)\cdot (-4\,i+2j) \\  & =-2t\cdot (-4)+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡((2t-1)\pi )\cdot 2 \\  & =8t+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡((2t-1)\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}8t+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡((2t-1)\pi )\,dt \\  & ={4{t}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡((2t-1)\pi )|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(4+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-(0+\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )) \\  & =(4+0)-(0+0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(3,2)$ to the point $B(1,5)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(3-2t)\,i+(2+3t)\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=3\,i+2\,j$ and $b=i+5\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(3\,i+2\,j)+t[(i+5\,j)-(3\,i+2\,j)] \\  & =(3\,i+2\,j)+t(-2\,i+3\,j) \\  & =(3-2t)\,i+(2+3t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3-2t,\,y=2+3t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j \\  & ={e}^{3-2t}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+3t)j \\  & =-2\,i+3\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{3-2t}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\,j)\cdot (-2\,i+3\,j) \\  & ={e}^{3-2t}\cdot (-2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\cdot 3 \\  & =-2{e}^{3-2t}+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2{e}^{3-2t}+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=2{x}^{7}\,i+{5}^{x+y}\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(2,3)$ to the point $B(5,4)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(2+3t)\,i+(3+t)\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=2\,i+3\,j$ and $b=5\,i+4\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(2\,i+3\,j)+t[(5\,i+4\,j)-(2\,i+3\,j)] \\  & =(2\,i+3\,j)+t(3\,i+j) \\  & =(2+3t)\,i+(3+t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2+3t,\,y=3+t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2{x}^{7}\,i+{5}^{x+y}\,j \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{2+3t+3+t}\,j \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{5+4t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3+t)j \\  & =3\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{5+4t}\,j)\cdot (3\,i+j) \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\cdot 3+{5}^{5+4t}\cdot 1 \\  & =6(2+3t)^{7}+{5}^{5+4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6(2+3t)^{7}+{5}^{5+4t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(4,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=2\,i$ and $b=4\,i+2\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(2\,i)+t[(4\,i+2\,j)-(2\,i)] \\  & =(2\,i)+t(2\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(2t+2)\,i+2t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2t+2\,y=2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j \\  & ={e}^{2t}\,i+{e}^{2t+2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)j \\  & =2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{2t}\,i+{e}^{2t+2}\,j)\cdot (2\,i+2\,j) \\  & ={e}^{2t}\cdot 2+{e}^{2t+2}\cdot 2 \\  & =2{e}^{2t}(1+{e}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{e}^{2t}(1+{e}^{2})\,dt \\  & =(1+{e}^{2}){e}^{2t}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+{e}^{2})({e}^{2}-1) \\  & ={e}^{4}-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=\frac{1}{x+y}\,i+\frac{2y}{x+y}\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(3,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=j$ and $b=3\,i.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(j)+t(3\,i-j) \\  & =3t\,i+(1-t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3t\,y=1-t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{x+y}\,i+\frac{2y}{x+y}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{3t+1-t}\,i+\frac{2-2t}{3t+1-t}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2t+1}\,i+\frac{2-2t}{2t+1}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)j \\  & =3\,i-j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{2t+1}\,i+\frac{2-2t}{2t+1}\,j)\cdot (3\,i-j) \\  & =\frac{1}{2t+1}\cdot 3+\frac{2-2t}{2t+1}\cdot (-1) \\  & =\frac{3-2+2t}{2t+1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1\,dt \\  & =t{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=y\,i+x\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $\operatorname{sin}⁡y=x-2$ traversed from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(2,\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡y=x-2\,⟹\,x=\operatorname{sin}⁡y+2.
$$

So, the parametrization of the curve is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le \pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j \\  & =t\,i+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2)\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+j) \\  & =t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2)\,dt \\  & ={[t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2t]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+2\pi )-0 \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=2{y}^{2}\,i+x\,j$ and $C$ is the curve ${y}^{2}=\frac{x-1}{3}$ traversed from the point $A(1,0)$ to the point $B(4,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
{y}^{2}=\frac{x-1}{3}\,⟹\,x=3{y}^{2}+1.
$$

So, the parametrization of the curve is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(3{t}^{2}+1)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3{t}^{2}+1,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2{y}^{2}\,i+x\,j \\  & =2{t}^{2}\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =6t\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2{t}^{2}\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j)\cdot (6t\,i+j) \\  & =2{t}^{2}\cdot 6t+(3{t}^{2}+1)\cdot 1 \\  & =12{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(12{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}+1)\,dt \\  & ={[3{t}^{4}+{t}^{3}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3+1+1-0 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ and $C$ is the curve ${y}^{3}=x+3$ traversed from the point $A(-3,0)$ to the point $B(5,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
{y}^{3}=x+3\,⟹\,x={y}^{3}-3.
$$

So, the parametrization of the curve is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =({t}^{3}-3)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{3}-3,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =({t}^{3}-3)\,i+{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(({t}^{3}-3))i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =3{t}^{2}i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(({t}^{3}-3)\,i+{t}^{2}\,j)\cdot (3{t}^{2}\,i+j) \\  & =({t}^{3}-3)\cdot 3{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =3{t}^{5}-9{t}^{2}+{t}^{2} \\  & =3{t}^{5}-8{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{t}^{5}-8{t}^{2})\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{6}}{2}-\frac{8{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{{2}^{6}}{2}-\frac{8(2)^{3}}{3})-0 \\  & =32-\frac{64}{3} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,i+y\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡x$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to the point $B(\frac{\pi }{2},2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Since $y$ is the subject of the equation, a parametrization is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+2{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=2{sin}^{2}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{sin}^{2}⁡t)j \\  & =i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2{sin}^{2}⁡t\text{ })\cdot (i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+8{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+8{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={[\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2{sin}^{4}⁡t]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $y=3{x}^{2}+1$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(1,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Since $y$ is the subject of the equation, a parametrization is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=3{t}^{2}+1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =t\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+1)j \\  & =i+6t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j)\cdot (i+6t\,j) \\  & =t\cdot 1+(3{t}^{2}+1)\cdot 6t \\  & =t+18{t}^{3}+6t \\  & =7t+18{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7t+18{t}^{3})\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{7{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{9{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{7(1)^{2}}{2}+\frac{9(1)^{4}}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{16}{2} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058907/assets/00ff3216e6876673a388eb3eaa0e7d02e268f5e679593ebd9fe01e2840099e1b.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+xy\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,2)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+xy\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(y-x)\,i-x\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=2$  traversed counterclockwise from the point $(\sqrt{2},0)$ to the point $(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)\,i-x\,j \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\sqrt{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}t]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x+y)\,i+(1-x)\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36$  traversed from the point $A(0,3)$ to the point $B(-2,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $3$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(x+y)\,i+(1-x)\,j \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-6({sin}^{2}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-6)\,dt \\  & =[\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-6t]_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =[1+0-6\pi ]-[-1+3-3\pi ] \\  & =-1-3\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=3y\,i+2x\,j$ and $C$ is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3$ respectively, traversed anticlockwise from $A(0,3)$ to $B(-1,0)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3$ respectively. It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =3y\,i+2x\,j \\  & =9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\,i-{e}^{y}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i-{e}^{y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i-{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i-{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\,dt \\  & ={[{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}-{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi /2}-{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi /2}-({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}-{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}) \\  & =1-e-(e-1) \\  & =2-2e\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) =(1-y)^2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(0, 2)$ to the point $B(1,0).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{i}.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =2j+t[i-2j] \\  & =t\,i+(2-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t = 1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
	y = 2-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(1-y)^{2}\,i+x\,j \\  & =(1-(2-2t))^{2}\,i+t\,j \\  & =(2t-1)^{2}\,i+t\,j \\  & =(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-2t)j \\  & =i-2j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i-2j) \\  & =(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\cdot (1)+(t)\cdot (-2) \\  & =4{t}^{2}-6t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}-6t+1\,dt \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}-3+1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = y\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is the curve $y^3 = x-5$ traversed from the point $A(5,0)$ to the point $B(6,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
y^3 = x-5
\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
x = y^3 + 5.
$$

So, we can parametrize the curve using

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =({t}^{3}+5)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t^3+5, \qquad
y = t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j \\  & =t\,i+({t}^{3}+5)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+5)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =3{t}^{2}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+({t}^{3}+5)\,j)\cdot (3{t}^{2}\,i+j) \\  & =t\cdot 3{t}^{2}+({t}^{3}+5)\cdot 1 \\  & =3{t}^{3}+{t}^{3}+5 \\  & =4{t}^{3}+5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{3}+5\,dt \\  & ={[{t}^{4}+5t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1+5-0 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = y\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The notation $\displaystyle\oint$ is used to remind us that we're dealing with a line integral over a *closed* curve.

We will use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \lt 2\pi.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad
y = \sin{t}.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t)+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
